1632.document_title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
1632.heading: Chapter X – Other Instructions
1632.text:
61. Secrecy Obligations and Sharing of Information:
(1) The NBFC shall maintain secrecy regarding the customer information that
arises out of the contractual relationship between the NBFC and the customer.
(2) The NBFC shall treat information collected from customers for the purpose of
opening of account as confidential and shall not divulge details thereof for the purpose
of cross-selling, or for any other purpose without the express permission of the
customer.
(3) While considering the requests for data / information from Government and
other agencies, the NBFC shall satisfy itself that the information being sought is not
of such a nature as will violate the provisions of the laws relating to secrecy in the
transactions.
(4) The exceptions to the said rule shall be as under:
(i) Where disclosure is under compulsion of law,
(ii) Where there is a duty to the public to disclose,
(iii) Where the interest of the NBFC requires disclosure, and
(iv) Where the disclosure is made with the express or implied consent of the
customer.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: An NBFC must ensure its digital lending app (and its LSP's app) does not access mobile phone resources such as the contact list, files and media, call logs or telephony functions. Only one-time access to camera, microphone or location is allowed, for onboarding/KYC, with explicit consent.
findings.recommendation: Remove the contact-list permission from the app at sign-up. Delete any contact data already collected. Audit the app and any LSP apps so none request contacts, files, call logs or telephony access.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: The NBFC must ensure that it and its agents do not intimidate or harass anyone in debt collection. This includes acts that intrude on the privacy of the debtor's family members, referees and friends, and sending inappropriate messages on mobile or social media. Undue harassment in recovery is also prohibited under the Fair Practices Code.
findings.recommendation: Stop the recovery team from calling or messaging people in the borrower's contact list. Limit recovery contact to the borrower, and to guarantors or co-obligors where applicable. Observe the calling-hour limits (8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.) and bar any message that tells third parties about the borrower's debt.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: The NBFC must keep customer information confidential and may not divulge it for any other purpose without the customer's express permission. Recovery agents must observe strict customer confidentiality. Explicit consent is also needed before sharing a borrower's personal information with a third party, unless a statutory or regulatory requirement applies.
findings.recommendation: Do not tell contacts that the borrower owes money or is in default. Disclose a borrower's debt status only with the borrower's explicit consent, or where the law requires it. Add confidentiality terms to recovery-agent scripts and contracts, and monitor compliance.

findings.document: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
findings.obligation: The notice to a Data Principal must give an itemised description of the personal data and the specified purpose. It must also explain how to withdraw consent and exercise rights. Collecting contact data, which holds third parties' personal data, without a notice that meets these requirements would fail them. Separately, data collection by a digital lending app must be need-based, with prior and explicit consent that has an audit trail.
findings.recommendation: Stop collecting contacts. If any contact data is retained, check whether a compliant notice and consent exist for it. The third parties whose numbers sit in the borrower's contacts have received no notice, so remove those records.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: Consent must be need-based, and the purpose for which consent is sought must be disclosed at each stage of the borrower interface. The borrower must be able to give or deny consent for specific data uses and to restrict disclosure to third parties. Contact-list data collected at sign-up and then used for recovery goes beyond a need-based, disclosed purpose.
findings.recommendation: Collect only the data needed for the stated lending purpose. Make sure each consent screen states its purpose and lets the borrower deny or revoke consent for specific data. Do not repurpose sign-up data for recovery contact.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: The NBFC must ensure that recovery agents are trained in privacy of customer information and hours of calling, and that they follow the code of conduct. It must also tell the borrower who the authorised recovery agent is when a loan defaults and an agent is assigned.
findings.recommendation: Train recovery staff on privacy and permitted contact. Get a signed undertaking to the code of conduct from recovery agents. Tell the borrower the particulars of the assigned recovery agent. Set up a grievance process for recovery complaints.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

Our digital lending app asks for permission to read the borrower's phone contacts at sign-up. If a loan becomes overdue, our recovery team calls and messages people in the contact list to remind them that the borrower owes us money.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Are digital lending apps of NBFCs permitted to access a borrower's phone contacts, and what limits apply to the mobile phone resources (contacts, files, call logs, telephony functions) an app may access?
- **q2** May an NBFC or its recovery agents contact persons in the borrower's contact list (third parties other than guarantors or co-obligors) about an overdue loan, and does this amount to harassment or intimidation under recovery conduct rules?
- **q3** Does disclosing the borrower's debt or default to people in the contact list violate the confidentiality obligations or the rules on the borrower's personal data held by the NBFC?
- **q4** What consent and notice requirements apply under the DPDP Rules for collecting contact list data, which includes personal data of third parties who are not the borrower, and for using it for recovery?
- **q5** Does the DPDP framework limit processing of personal data to the purpose stated at collection and require data minimisation, and is using contact data for debt recovery consistent with a purpose stated at sign-up?
- **q6** What rules govern the conduct of recovery agents and the borrower's grievance rights, including standards for agent communications and the need for borrower-facing disclosure of recovery practices?

## Findings (6)

### 1. [HIGH] An NBFC must ensure its digital lending app (and its LSP's app) does not access mobile phone resources such as the contact list, files and media, call logs or telephony functions. Only one-time access to camera, microphone or location is allowed, for onboarding/KYC, with explicit consent.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Remove the contact-list permission from the app at sign-up. Delete any contact data already collected. Audit the app and any LSP apps so none request contacts, files, call logs or telephony access.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

### 2. [HIGH] The NBFC must ensure that it and its agents do not intimidate or harass anyone in debt collection. This includes acts that intrude on the privacy of the debtor's family members, referees and friends, and sending inappropriate messages on mobile or social media. Undue harassment in recovery is also prohibited under the Fair Practices Code.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Stop the recovery team from calling or messaging people in the borrower's contact list. Limit recovery contact to the borrower, and to guarantors or co-obligors where applicable. Observe the calling-hour limits (8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.) and bar any message that tells third parties about the borrower's debt.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 100, pp. 28-29 (passage 2158)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 20, p. 8 (passage 2072)

### 3. [HIGH] The NBFC must keep customer information confidential and may not divulge it for any other purpose without the customer's express permission. Recovery agents must observe strict customer confidentiality. Explicit consent is also needed before sharing a borrower's personal information with a third party, unless a statutory or regulatory requirement applies.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Do not tell contacts that the borrower owes money or is in default. Disclose a borrower's debt status only with the borrower's explicit consent, or where the law requires it. Add confidentiality terms to recovery-agent scripts and contracts, and monitor compliance.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 61, p. 56 (passage 1632)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 99, p. 28 (passage 2157)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

### 4. [HIGH] The notice to a Data Principal must give an itemised description of the personal data and the specified purpose. It must also explain how to withdraw consent and exercise rights. Collecting contact data, which holds third parties' personal data, without a notice that meets these requirements would fail them. Separately, data collection by a digital lending app must be need-based, with prior and explicit consent that has an audit trail.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Stop collecting contacts. If any contact data is retained, check whether a compliant notice and consent exist for it. The third parties whose numbers sit in the borrower's contacts have received no notice, so remove those records.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 3, pp. 24-25 (passage 1962)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

### 5. [MEDIUM] Consent must be need-based, and the purpose for which consent is sought must be disclosed at each stage of the borrower interface. The borrower must be able to give or deny consent for specific data uses and to restrict disclosure to third parties. Contact-list data collected at sign-up and then used for recovery goes beyond a need-based, disclosed purpose.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Collect only the data needed for the stated lending purpose. Make sure each consent screen states its purpose and lets the borrower deny or revoke consent for specific data. Do not repurpose sign-up data for recovery contact.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

### 6. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must ensure that recovery agents are trained in privacy of customer information and hours of calling, and that they follow the code of conduct. It must also tell the borrower who the authorised recovery agent is when a loan defaults and an agent is assigned.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: Train recovery staff on privacy and permitted contact. Get a signed undertaking to the code of conduct from recovery agents. Tell the borrower the particulars of the assigned recovery agent. Set up a grievance process for recovery complaints.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 98, p. 28 (passage 2156)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 99, p. 28 (passage 2157)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 9, part 2 of 2, p. 17 (passage 1723)

1719.document_title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
1719.heading: Chapter III – Digital Lending › A. General Requirements for NBFC-LSP Arrangements
1719.text:
6. Due diligence requirements with respect to LSPs
(1) Digital lending by an NBFC involving a LSP, shall be carried out under a
contractual agreement between the NBFC and the LSP, which clearly defines
the respective roles, rights, and obligations of each party thereto.
(2) An NBFC shall conduct enhanced due diligence before they enter into an
agreement with a LSP for digital lending, taking into account LSP’s technical
capabilities, robustness of data privacy policies and storage systems, fairness
in conduct with borrowers, past records of conduct and ability to comply with
all applicable regulations and statutes.
(3) An NBFC shall carry out periodic review of the conduct of the LSP vis-à-vis the
terms of the contractual agreement and shall take appropriate action in the
event of any deviation therefrom.
(4) An NBFC shall lay down, as part of its policy, suitable monitoring mechanisms
for the loan portfolios originated with the support of LSPs.
(5) An NBFC shall impart necessary guidance to LSP acting as a recovery agent,
to discharge their duties responsibly and ensure that LSP complies with the
applicable instructions under Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial
Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, and other
relevant instructions as issued from time to time.
(6) An NBFC shall continue to conform to the extant guidelines on outsourcing (as
specified under Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies –
Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025) and shall ensure that the
LSPs engaged by them and the DLAs (either of the NBFC or of the LSPs
engaged by the NBFC) comply with these Directions.
(7) As an overarching principle, any outsourcing agreement entered into by an
NBFC with an LSP shall in no manner dilute or absolve the NBFC of its
obligations under any statutory or regulatory provision, and the NBFC shall
remain fully responsible and liable for all acts and omissions of the LSP.

(1) An NBFC shall ensure that LSP engaged by them do not store personal

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: An NBFC must ensure all data is stored only on servers located within India. Data processed outside India must be deleted from foreign servers and brought back to India within 24 hours of processing.
findings.recommendation: Move all borrower data, including bank statements and KYC documents, to servers located in India. Do not use the Singapore cloud region for storage. If any processing happens abroad, delete the data there and return it to India within 24 hours. Weigh cost against this hard localisation requirement.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: Data collection by the DLA must be need-based, with prior explicit consent and an audit trail. Borrowers must be able to deny or revoke consent, restrict disclosure and retention, and ask for deletion. The purpose must be disclosed at each stage. LSPs may store only minimal basic personal data, and the NBFC stays responsible for privacy and security.
findings.recommendation: Check that each data item stored, including bank statements, is need-based and covered by explicit, purpose-specific consent with an audit trail. Provide consent withdrawal and deletion controls. Confirm that any LSP holds only minimal data. Publish a storage policy covering data types, retention, destruction and breach handling.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: The NBFC must preserve customer identification records and transaction records for at least five years after the relationship ends. It must be able to retrieve them quickly and give them to competent authorities promptly on request. The passage sets no location rule of its own, but the digital lending directions require data to be held on servers in India.
findings.recommendation: Make sure KYC records held in Singapore can be retrieved quickly and produced on request. Moving them to India-located servers resolves both the retrieval concern and the localisation issue. Set retention to at least five years after the relationship ends.

findings.document: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
findings.obligation: Personal data may be transferred outside India, but the Data Fiduciary must meet any requirements the Central Government specifies for making the data available to a foreign State or its entities or agencies.
findings.recommendation: Track any government orders under Rule 15 that apply to the Singapore storage. Note that the RBI localisation requirement is stricter than the DPDP transfer rule and still applies.

findings.document: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
findings.obligation: The Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards, including for processing by a Data Processor. These include encryption or masking, access controls, logging and monitoring, backups, one-year log retention, and contract terms with the processor on security. On a breach it must notify each affected Data Principal without delay and notify the Board, with a detailed report within 72 hours.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

Our digital lending app stores all borrower data, including bank statements and KYC documents, on a cloud region in Singapore to reduce cost.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Do the RBI digital lending directions require that data collected by a lending service provider or digital lending app be stored on servers located in India, and do they restrict storing borrower data in a cloud region outside India?
- **q2** Do the RBI digital lending directions limit what borrower data an NBFC or its digital lending app may collect and store, such as bank statements, and what consent and purpose limits apply?
- **q3** Do the RBI KYC Directions place restrictions on where KYC records and customer identification documents are maintained, and what record retention and access requirements apply to them?
- **q4** Do the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025 restrict or condition the transfer of personal data outside India by a data fiduciary, and are there any additional requirements for such transfers?
- **q5** What reasonable security safeguards and breach intimation duties do the DPDP Rules 2025 impose on an NBFC as data fiduciary when a data processor such as a cloud provider holds borrower data?
- **q6** Do the RBI digital lending directions make the NBFC responsible for the conduct of lending service providers and cloud or third-party processors holding borrower data, and what disclosure to borrowers is required about such data handling?

## Findings (6)

### 1. [HIGH] An NBFC must ensure all data is stored only on servers located within India. Data processed outside India must be deleted from foreign servers and brought back to India within 24 hours of processing.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Move all borrower data, including bank statements and KYC documents, to servers located in India. Do not use the Singapore cloud region for storage. If any processing happens abroad, delete the data there and return it to India within 24 hours. Weigh cost against this hard localisation requirement.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)

### 2. [MEDIUM] Data collection by the DLA must be need-based, with prior explicit consent and an audit trail. Borrowers must be able to deny or revoke consent, restrict disclosure and retention, and ask for deletion. The purpose must be disclosed at each stage. LSPs may store only minimal basic personal data, and the NBFC stays responsible for privacy and security.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Check that each data item stored, including bank statements, is need-based and covered by explicit, purpose-specific consent with an audit trail. Provide consent withdrawal and deletion controls. Confirm that any LSP holds only minimal data. Publish a storage policy covering data types, retention, destruction and breach handling.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)

### 3. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must preserve customer identification records and transaction records for at least five years after the relationship ends. It must be able to retrieve them quickly and give them to competent authorities promptly on request. The passage sets no location rule of its own, but the digital lending directions require data to be held on servers in India.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Make sure KYC records held in Singapore can be retrieved quickly and produced on request. Moving them to India-located servers resolves both the retrieval concern and the localisation issue. Set retention to at least five years after the relationship ends.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 47, pp. 48-49 (passage 1616)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)

### 4. [MEDIUM] The Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards, including for processing by a Data Processor. These include encryption or masking, access controls, logging and monitoring, backups, one-year log retention, and contract terms with the processor on security. On a breach it must notify each affected Data Principal without delay and notify the Board, with a detailed report within 72 hours.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Confirm that the cloud contract includes security safeguards, access control, logging and backups. Encrypt the stored data. Set up a breach-response process that can notify borrowers and the Board within the required timelines, including when the breach occurs at the cloud provider.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 6, p. 26 (passage 1965)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 7, p. 26 (passage 1966)

### 5. [MEDIUM] The NBFC remains fully responsible and liable for the acts and omissions of its LSPs. It must carry out due diligence on the LSP's data privacy and storage systems and review its conduct periodically. It must publicly disclose its data storage policy and privacy policy on its website and DLA.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: Treat the cloud provider and any LSP as under the NBFC's accountability. Assess their storage systems and review their conduct periodically. Make sure the published privacy and storage policies accurately describe where and how data is stored.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 6, p. 14 (passage 1719)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 15, pp. 20-21 (passage 1730)

### 6. [LOW] Personal data may be transferred outside India, but the Data Fiduciary must meet any requirements the Central Government specifies for making the data available to a foreign State or its entities or agencies.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Track any government orders under Rule 15 that apply to the Singapore storage. Note that the RBI localisation requirement is stricter than the DPDP transfer rule and still applies.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 15, p. 30 (passage 1978)

## Research limits reached

- q2: stopped after 4 research turns.

1719.document_title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
1719.heading: Chapter III – Digital Lending › A. General Requirements for NBFC-LSP Arrangements
1719.text:
6. Due diligence requirements with respect to LSPs
(1) Digital lending by an NBFC involving a LSP, shall be carried out under a
contractual agreement between the NBFC and the LSP, which clearly defines
the respective roles, rights, and obligations of each party thereto.
(2) An NBFC shall conduct enhanced due diligence before they enter into an
agreement with a LSP for digital lending, taking into account LSP’s technical
capabilities, robustness of data privacy policies and storage systems, fairness
in conduct with borrowers, past records of conduct and ability to comply with
all applicable regulations and statutes.
(3) An NBFC shall carry out periodic review of the conduct of the LSP vis-à-vis the
terms of the contractual agreement and shall take appropriate action in the
event of any deviation therefrom.
(4) An NBFC shall lay down, as part of its policy, suitable monitoring mechanisms
for the loan portfolios originated with the support of LSPs.
(5) An NBFC shall impart necessary guidance to LSP acting as a recovery agent,
to discharge their duties responsibly and ensure that LSP complies with the
applicable instructions under Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial
Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, and other
relevant instructions as issued from time to time.
(6) An NBFC shall continue to conform to the extant guidelines on outsourcing (as
specified under Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies –
Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025) and shall ensure that the
LSPs engaged by them and the DLAs (either of the NBFC or of the LSPs
engaged by the NBFC) comply with these Directions.
(7) As an overarching principle, any outsourcing agreement entered into by an
NBFC with an LSP shall in no manner dilute or absolve the NBFC of its
obligations under any statutory or regulatory provision, and the NBFC shall
remain fully responsible and liable for all acts and omissions of the LSP.

1724.heading: Chapter III – Digital Lending › B. Conduct and Customer Protection Requirements
1724.text:
10. Loan disbursal, servicing and repayment
(1) Disbursement of loan by an NBFC shall always be made into the bank account
of the borrower except for disbursals covered exclusively under statutory or
regulatory mandate (of the Reserve Bank or of any other regulator), flow of
money between lenders for co-lending transactions and disbursals for specific
end use, provided the loan is disbursed directly into the bank account of the
end-beneficiary. An NBFC shall ensure that in no case, disbursal is made to a
third-party account, including the accounts of LSP, except as provided for in
this Chapter on ‘Digital Lending’.
Provided that advances against salary, where the loan is disbursed directly to
the bank account of the borrower, but the repayment is from the corporate
employer, can be allowed subject to the condition that the loan is repaid by the
corporate employer by deducting the amount from the borrower’s salary.
However, it must be ensured that LSPs do not have any control over the flow
of funds directly or indirectly in such transactions and that repayment is directly
from the bank account of the employer to the NBFC.
Note: Co-lending arrangements shall be governed by the Reserve Bank of
India (Non- Banking Financial Companies – Transfer and Distribution of Credit
Risk) Directions, 2025, subject to the condition that no third party other than
the lenders in a co-lending transaction shall have direct or indirect control over
the flow of funds at any point of time.
(2) An NBFC shall ensure that all loan servicing, repayment, etc. is executed by
the borrower directly in the NBFC’s bank account without any pass-through
account/ pool account of any third party, including the accounts of LSP.
(3) The flow of funds between the bank accounts of the borrower and the NBFC
shall not be controlled either directly or indirectly by a third-party, including the
LSP.

findings.recommendation: Stop disbursing into the LSP's pool account. Disburse directly into each borrower's bank account and make sure the LSP has no direct or indirect control over the flow of funds.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: The KFS must show the sanctioned amount, fees payable to the NBFC and to third parties routed through the NBFC, and the net disbursed amount. findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025

The NBFC remains fully responsible for the LSP's acts and omissions.
findings.recommendation: Review the LSP agreement and due diligence file. Add controls and monitoring so the LSP cannot hold or deduct borrower funds, and take action on the deviation already seen in the pool-account and fee-deduction flow.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: Loan servicing and repayment must go directly into the NBFC's bank account, without any pass-through or pool account of a third party, including the LSP. Flows of funds between the borrower and NBFC bank accounts must not be controlled directly or indirectly by the LSP. The pool-account model cannot be reconciled with these rules.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

For loans sourced through our lending service provider's app, we disburse the loan amount into the LSP's pool account, and the LSP transfers it to the borrower after deducting its own service fee.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Do the RBI digital lending rules allow an NBFC to disburse a loan into an LSP's pool account instead of directly into the borrower's bank account?
- **q2** May a lending service provider deduct its own service fee from the loan amount before it reaches the borrower, or must the NBFC pay the LSP's fees and charges itself?
- **q3** How must the loan amount, LSP fees and other charges be shown in the key facts statement and the net disbursed amount and APR calculated when deductions are made at disbursement?
- **q4** What are the NBFC's responsibilities for the conduct, outsourcing oversight and due diligence of the LSP that handles borrower funds?
- **q5** What flow of funds and record-keeping requirements apply to repayments and disbursements in digital lending, and how can the pool-account arrangement be reconciled with them?

## Findings (5)

### 1. [HIGH] An NBFC must always disburse a loan into the borrower's bank account. Narrow exceptions apply: statutory or regulatory mandates, co-lending flows between lenders, and specific end-use disbursals paid directly to the end-beneficiary. Disbursal to a third-party account, including an LSP's account, is not permitted.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Stop disbursing into the LSP's pool account. Disburse directly into each borrower's bank account and make sure the LSP has no direct or indirect control over the flow of funds.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 10, part 1 of 2, pp. 17-18 (passage 1724)

### 2. [HIGH] Fees, charges and reimbursements payable to the LSP must be paid directly by the NBFC. The LSP must not charge or collect them from borrowers separately.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Remove the LSP's deduction of its service fee from the loan amount. Pay the LSP's fee from the NBFC's own funds under the contract and disburse the full net amount to the borrower.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 10, part 2 of 2, p. 18 (passage 1725)

### 3. [HIGH] Loan servicing and repayment must go directly into the NBFC's bank account, without any pass-through or pool account of a third party, including the LSP. Flows of funds between the borrower and NBFC bank accounts must not be controlled directly or indirectly by the LSP. The pool-account model cannot be reconciled with these rules.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Redesign disbursement and repayment flows so funds move only between the NBFC's and the borrower's bank accounts. Do not try to reconcile the pool-account arrangement. Remove it and confirm that repayments also bypass LSP accounts.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 10, part 1 of 2, pp. 17-18 (passage 1724)

### 4. [MEDIUM] The KFS must show the sanctioned amount, fees payable to the NBFC and to third parties routed through the NBFC, and the net disbursed amount. The APR is computed on the net disbursed amount using the IRR approach and reducing balance method. APR includes the interest rate and all other charges associated with the credit facility.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Make sure the KFS and APR calculation reflect the actual charges and net disbursed amount. Once the LSP fee is paid by the NBFC and not deducted from the borrower, check that the KFS does not misstate net disbursal or APR.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 29, part 2 of 3, pp. 11-12 (passage 2082)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 6, part 1 of 2, pp. 4-5 (passage 2056)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 9, part 1 of 2, pp. 16-17 (passage 1722)

### 5. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must have a contractual agreement defining roles with the LSP and conduct enhanced due diligence before engaging it. It must review the LSP's conduct periodically and monitor LSP-originated portfolios. It must follow the outsourcing directions and ensure the LSP complies with these Directions. The NBFC remains fully responsible for the LSP's acts and omissions.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Review the LSP agreement and due diligence file. Add controls and monitoring so the LSP cannot hold or deduct borrower funds, and take action on the deviation already seen in the pool-account and fee-deduction flow.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 6, p. 14 (passage 1719)

11. Cooling-off period
(1) The borrower shall be given an explicit option to exit a digital loan by paying

exits the loan during the cooling-off period. This, if applicable, shall be
disclosed to the customer upfront in KFS.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

Once a digital loan is disbursed it cannot be cancelled. A borrower who wants to exit early pays the full foreclosure charge of 3% of the principal, even on the day after disbursal.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Must a digital loan borrower be given a cooling-off or look-up period after disbursal during which they can exit the loan by repaying only the principal and proportionate APR, without penalty?
- **q2** Are NBFCs restricted from levying foreclosure or pre-payment charges on certain borrowers or loan types, such as floating rate loans to individual borrowers, and does a flat 3% charge on principal comply?
- **q3** Must the foreclosure or pre-payment charge be disclosed upfront in the Key Facts Statement and loan agreement before the borrower accepts the loan, and how should it be presented?
- **q4** Are there requirements that charges be reasonable, transparent and not levied without being disclosed, and that fair practice terms not be unfair to the borrower?

## Findings (4)

### 1. [HIGH] A digital loan borrower must be given an explicit option to exit during a cooling-off period of at least one day by paying only the principal and proportionate APR, without penalty. The NBFC may retain only a reasonable one-time processing fee, disclosed upfront in the KFS.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Remove the no-cancellation rule and the 3% charge for early exit. Build a cooling-off exit of at least one day where the borrower repays principal plus proportionate APR, with at most a reasonable one-time processing fee disclosed in the KFS. Exits the day after disbursal must fall inside this window unless the credit policy sets a longer one.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 11, p. 18 (passage 1726)

### 2. [MEDIUM] No pre-payment charges may be levied on floating rate loans for non-business purposes to individuals (existing loans under Para 33, and loans sanctioned or renewed from 1 January 2026 under Para 34(1)). Business-purpose floating rate loans to individuals and MSEs are also barred from charges, depending on NBFC layer and loan size. Microfinance loans cannot carry any pre-payment charge. In other cases, charges follow the approved policy and, for term loans, must be based on the amount being prepaid. No charge may be levied where pre-payment is at the NBFC's instance.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: The feature does not say whether loans are floating or fixed rate, personal or business, or microfinance. Check each loan product against these prohibitions and switch off the 3% charge where it is barred. Where a charge is allowed, make sure it is covered by the Board-approved policy and is levied on the amount prepaid. Also confirm no charge applies when the NBFC initiates the pre-payment.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 34, part 1 of 2, pp. 17-18 (passage 2091)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 33, p. 17 (passage 2090)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 81, p. 26 (passage 2139)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 34, part 2 of 2, p. 18 (passage 2092)

### 3. [MEDIUM] The applicability of pre-payment charges must be clearly disclosed in the sanction letter and loan agreement, and in the KFS where one is required. Foreclosure charges appear under contingent charges in the KFS format. No undisclosed pre-payment charge may be levied.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Show the 3% foreclosure charge, and the cases where it applies, in the sanction letter, loan agreement and KFS (contingent charges, item 10(iii)) before the borrower accepts. Block any levy that was not disclosed in this way.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 34, part 2 of 2, p. 18 (passage 2092)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Annex I, part 1 of 2, pp. 34-35 (passage 2169)

### 4. [LOW] Fair practice requires that loan terms and conditions be conveyed in writing, and that a copy of the loan agreement and its enclosures be given to the borrower at sanction or disbursement. Failing to do so is an unfair practice. The Reserve Bank has also flagged excessive interest and charges as a concern.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Make sure the no-cancellation term and the 3% foreclosure charge are plainly stated in the borrower's agreement copy. Review whether a full 3% charge the day after disbursal is reasonable under the fair practices code and the Board's charges policy.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 14, pp. 7-8 (passage 2066)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 25, p. 9 (passage 2077)

## Research limits reached

- q4: stopped after 4 research turns.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

If our customer database is breached, our incident plan is to email affected customers within 30 days once the investigation is complete. We do not plan to inform any regulator or board.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025, what is the Data Fiduciary's obligation to notify the Data Protection Board of India of a personal data breach, and within what timelines must the intimation and detailed report be made?
- **q2** Under the DPDP Rules 2025, what must a Data Fiduciary tell each affected Data Principal about a personal data breach, and how quickly must the notice be given?
- **q3** What reasonable security safeguards must a Data Fiduciary maintain under the DPDP Rules 2025 to detect, investigate and remediate a personal data breach, including logging, monitoring and retention of logs?
- **q4** Do the RBI Directions for NBFCs on digital lending require the NBFC to maintain data security and privacy controls for borrower data held by it or its lending service providers, and do they require any incident reporting or board oversight?
- **q5** Do the RBI NBFC KYC Directions 2025 impose confidentiality and security requirements on customer KYC records, and are there any obligations in the event KYC data is compromised?

## Findings (5)

### 1. [HIGH] On becoming aware of a personal data breach, the Data Fiduciary must intimate the Data Protection Board without delay with a description of the breach, and within 72 hours (or a longer period the Board allows) give detailed information, including the facts, mitigation, findings on the cause, remedial measures and a report on intimations to Data Principals.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Change the incident plan to include notifying the Board without delay and filing the detailed report within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach. Assign an owner and prepare templates for both filings.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 7, p. 26 (passage 1966)

### 2. [HIGH] The Data Fiduciary must tell each affected Data Principal, without delay, about the breach: its nature, extent and timing, the likely consequences, the mitigation measures, the safety steps the person can take, and a business contact. The notice must be concise, clear and plain, and sent through the user account or a registered communication mode.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Replace the plan to wait 30 days until the investigation ends with notice to customers without delay on becoming aware of the breach. Use a notice template covering items (a) to (e), and send updates as the investigation progresses.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 7, p. 26 (passage 1966)

### 3. [MEDIUM] The Data Fiduciary must maintain reasonable security safeguards, at minimum including encryption or masking, access controls, logs, monitoring and review to detect and investigate unauthorised access, and data backups. It must also retain logs and personal data for one year to support detection, investigation and remediation, and must have appropriate contract terms with Data Processors.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: The plan describes no detection, logging or investigation capability. Confirm that logging, monitoring and review, one-year log retention, backups, access control and processor contract clauses are in place, so that a breach can be detected and investigated quickly.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 6, p. 26 (passage 1965)

### 4. [MEDIUM] The NBFC remains responsible for the data privacy and security of borrower personal information, including data held by its LSPs. It must have clear policies on data storage and on standards for handling a security breach, disclosed on its website and DLA. It must also ensure that it and its LSPs comply with RBI cybersecurity standards.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Write a breach-handling standard, publish it on the website and DLA, and cover LSPs. Align the incident plan with RBI cybersecurity requirements, since the current plan has no regulator or board escalation. The passages provided do not state a specific RBI incident-reporting timeline.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 16, p. 21 (passage 1731)

### 5. [LOW] Digital lending must be covered by a Board-approved credit policy. A breach plan that excludes the board from oversight is inconsistent with this governance requirement.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Check that the Board-approved digital lending policy covers data security and breach escalation, and add a path to inform the board of breaches.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 5, p. 13 (passage 1718)

findings.document: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
findings.obligation: A Data Fiduciary must adopt technical and organisational measures to obtain verifiable parental consent before processing any personal data of a child (under 18). A 13-17 year old cannot validly consent alone.
findings.recommendation: Redesign onboarding so a parent or guardian is identified and gives verifiable consent before any child data (name, date of birth, phone number) is processed. Do not allow self sign-up without this step.

findings.document: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
findings.obligation: The Data Fiduciary must check that the person claiming to be the parent is an identifiable adult. It does this using reliable identity and age details it already holds, or details voluntarily provided by the parent, including through a government-authorised entity's virtual token or a Digital Locker service provider.
findings.recommendation: Build a parent verification flow. For existing users, confirm the data held is reliable. For new parents, verify age and identity through government-issued details, a virtual token or DigiLocker before creating the child's account.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: When an NBFC establishes an account-based relationship, it must carry out CDD by obtaining Aadhaar or an OVD (or equivalent e-document, or KYC Identifier) and PAN or Form 60, and must verify these. Self-declared name, date of birth and phone number do not meet this. Minor-specific or guardian provisions are not stated in the passages given.
findings.recommendation: Confirm with compliance how KYC applies to minors and the guardian's role. Do not onboard minors on self-declared details alone. Obtain and verify the required identity documents, involving the guardian where the Directions require it.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: Verification must follow prescribed methods: offline verification of Aadhaar, digital signature verification of e-documents with a live photo, digital KYC, or CKYCR retrieval. A simplified procedure applies only where the person cannot produce the documents, and only under stated conditions.
findings.recommendation: Add an identity verification step (Aadhaar offline verification, OVD e-document, Digital KYC or V-CIP). Use the simplified procedure only if its conditions are met and documented.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: Accounts opened non-face-to-face (a remote app sign-up) are subject to enhanced due diligence. Such customers are categorised as high-risk, and the first transaction must be a credit from the customer's existing KYC-compliant bank account.
findings.recommendation: Apply EDD controls to remote onboarding. Fund the first transaction from an existing KYC-compliant account, and treat these accounts as high-risk with enhanced monitoring.

findings.document: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
findings.obligation: The child-data protections in section 9 (parental consent, no tracking or behavioural monitoring) are relaxed only for the listed purposes, such as real-time location for safety, or preventing access to harmful content. A pocket-money app's usage tracking or ad targeting is not among them.
findings.recommendation: Do not track, behaviourally monitor or target advertising at child users. Limit any processing to what the Fourth Schedule exemptions allow, and document the basis.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: If the card has any credit component, the NBFC must assess creditworthiness, including age, occupation and income, before extending a loan. It must also provide a Key Facts Statement with APR and all charges to the borrower. Credit card receivables are exempt from the KFS rules. The passages do not address capacity of minors.
findings.recommendation: Keep the product strictly prepaid or debit-like with no credit or overdraft for under-18s. If any credit or fee element is planned, obtain legal advice on contractual capacity, run the age, occupation and income assessment, and provide a KFS and clear charge disclosure.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

We are launching a pocket-money card and app for teenagers aged 13 to 17. They sign up themselves with their name, date of birth and phone number; parents are not involved.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Does the DPDP Act and Rules 2025 require verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian before processing personal data of a child under 18, and can a teenager aged 13 to 17 sign up on their own without parental involvement?
- **q2** How must a data fiduciary verify that the person giving consent for a child is an identifiable adult parent, and what means of verification are permitted?
- **q3** Does the DPDP framework prohibit tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children, and does it apply to usage data collected through the app and card?
- **q4** Can an NBFC onboard a minor as a customer for a card or prepaid-type product under the KYC Directions, and what customer identification and due diligence applies to a minor, including whether a guardian must be involved?
- **q5** Is collecting only name, date of birth and phone number sufficient to meet KYC requirements for onboarding, or are officially valid documents or other identity verification required?
- **q6** Are NBFCs permitted to extend credit or a credit-linked card to persons below 18 who lack contractual capacity, and what disclosures such as key facts statement and charges would apply if the card has any credit or fee component?

## Findings (7)

### 1. [HIGH] A Data Fiduciary must adopt technical and organisational measures to obtain verifiable parental consent before processing any personal data of a child (under 18). A 13-17 year old cannot validly consent alone.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Redesign onboarding so a parent or guardian is identified and gives verifiable consent before any child data (name, date of birth, phone number) is processed. Do not allow self sign-up without this step.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 10, part 1 of 3, pp. 27-28 (passage 1970)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 10, part 2 of 3, p. 28 (passage 1971)

### 2. [HIGH] The Data Fiduciary must check that the person claiming to be the parent is an identifiable adult. It does this using reliable identity and age details it already holds, or details voluntarily provided by the parent, including through a government-authorised entity's virtual token or a Digital Locker service provider.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Build a parent verification flow. For existing users, confirm the data held is reliable. For new parents, verify age and identity through government-issued details, a virtual token or DigiLocker before creating the child's account.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 10, part 3 of 3, p. 28 (passage 1972)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 10, part 2 of 3, p. 28 (passage 1971)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 10, part 1 of 3, pp. 27-28 (passage 1970)

### 3. [HIGH] When an NBFC establishes an account-based relationship, it must carry out CDD by obtaining Aadhaar or an OVD (or equivalent e-document, or KYC Identifier) and PAN or Form 60, and must verify these. Self-declared name, date of birth and phone number do not meet this. Minor-specific or guardian provisions are not stated in the passages given.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Confirm with compliance how KYC applies to minors and the guardian's role. Do not onboard minors on self-declared details alone. Obtain and verify the required identity documents, involving the guardian where the Directions require it.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 23, part 1 of 4, pp. 24-25 (passage 1576)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 23, part 2 of 4, p. 25 (passage 1577)

### 4. [HIGH] Verification must follow prescribed methods: offline verification of Aadhaar, digital signature verification of e-documents with a live photo, digital KYC, or CKYCR retrieval. A simplified procedure applies only where the person cannot produce the documents, and only under stated conditions.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Add an identity verification step (Aadhaar offline verification, OVD e-document, Digital KYC or V-CIP). Use the simplified procedure only if its conditions are met and documented.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 23, part 2 of 4, p. 25 (passage 1577)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 28, pp. 34-35 (passage 1592)

### 5. [MEDIUM] The child-data protections in section 9 (parental consent, no tracking or behavioural monitoring) are relaxed only for the listed purposes, such as real-time location for safety, or preventing access to harmful content. A pocket-money app's usage tracking or ad targeting is not among them.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Do not track, behaviourally monitor or target advertising at child users. Limit any processing to what the Fourth Schedule exemptions allow, and document the basis.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Fourth Schedule, Part B, Item 5, p. 37 (passage 2027)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Fourth Schedule, Part B, p. 37 (passage 2022)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Fourth Schedule, Part B, Item 4, p. 37 (passage 2026)

### 6. [MEDIUM] Accounts opened non-face-to-face (a remote app sign-up) are subject to enhanced due diligence. Such customers are categorised as high-risk, and the first transaction must be a credit from the customer's existing KYC-compliant bank account.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Apply EDD controls to remote onboarding. Fund the first transaction from an existing KYC-compliant account, and treat these accounts as high-risk with enhanced monitoring.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 44, part 2 of 2, p. 46 (passage 1613)

### 7. [MEDIUM] If the card has any credit component, the NBFC must assess creditworthiness, including age, occupation and income, before extending a loan. It must also provide a Key Facts Statement with APR and all charges to the borrower. Credit card receivables are exempt from the KFS rules. The passages do not address capacity of minors.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: Keep the product strictly prepaid or debit-like with no credit or overdraft for under-18s. If any credit or fee element is planned, obtain legal advice on contractual capacity, run the age, occupation and income assessment, and provide a KFS and clear charge disclosure.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 8, pp. 15-16 (passage 1721)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 9, part 1 of 2, pp. 16-17 (passage 1722)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 29, part 1 of 3, pp. 10-11 (passage 2081)

## Research limits reached

- q4: stopped after 4 research turns.
- q5: stopped after 4 research turns.
- Tool-call budget (20) reached; research stopped before q6.

1616.text:

(iii) the date on which the transaction was conducted; and
(iv) the parties to the transaction.
(6) evolve a system for proper maintenance and preservation of account
information in a manner that allows the NBFC to retrieve data easily and quickly
whenever required or when competent authorities request it;

respect of transactions referred to in Rule 3 in hard or soft format.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

During onboarding we photograph the customer's Aadhaar card (front and back) and keep the unmasked images in our cloud bucket indefinitely, so that periodic re-KYC can reuse them. Branch staff can download them from the admin portal.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Are NBFCs permitted to capture and store the full unmasked Aadhaar number or Aadhaar card images, or must the Aadhaar number be redacted or blacked out when a copy of the Aadhaar is collected for KYC?
- **q2** For how long must an NBFC retain KYC records and customer identification documents, and from when does this retention period run (business relationship end vs. account closure)?
- **q3** Must personal data such as Aadhaar images be erased once the specified purpose is no longer served, and what retention limits apply to personal data held by a Data Fiduciary after the purpose is fulfilled?
- **q4** What reasonable security safeguards must the NBFC apply to personal data in cloud storage and to staff access, such as encryption, access control, logging and monitoring of access to stored Aadhaar images?
- **q5** Can previously collected KYC documents be reused for periodic re-KYC, or does the regulation require fresh or updated customer due diligence, and what are the permitted modes of re-KYC and record updating?
- **q6** What notice and consent must be obtained from the customer before collecting and retaining Aadhaar images, including the specific purpose, itemised data and retention described in the notice?

## Findings (5)

### 1. [HIGH] Where Aadhaar authentication is not required, the NBFC must have the customer black out the Aadhaar number through appropriate means. The same redaction applies in V-CIP. Aadhaar use must also follow the Aadhaar Act and its regulations.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Stop storing unmasked Aadhaar images. Redact or black out the Aadhaar number at capture unless authentication is required, and mask existing stored images. Confirm the flow against the Aadhaar Act and regulations.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 23, part 4 of 4, p. 26 (passage 1579)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 27, part 4 of 5, pp. 33-34 (passage 1590)

### 2. [MEDIUM] A Data Fiduciary must retain personal data and processing logs for a minimum of one year and then erase them, unless another law requires longer retention. Indefinite retention of unmasked Aadhaar images has no basis beyond the legal retention requirement.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Define a retention and erasure policy that ties retention to the KYC record-keeping period. Erase the images and logs once that period ends, and do not keep them indefinitely.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 8, part 2 of 2, p. 27 (passage 1968)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 47, pp. 48-49 (passage 1616)

### 3. [MEDIUM] The Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards, at a minimum: encryption, obfuscation or masking; access controls; logs, monitoring and review of access to personal data; backups; one-year log retention; and contractual safeguards with processors.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Encrypt the cloud bucket and restrict access by role. Disable bulk or branch-level downloads unless they are necessary. Log and review every access to Aadhaar images and keep the logs for at least one year. Ensure the cloud provider contract carries security obligations.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 6, p. 26 (passage 1965)

### 4. [MEDIUM] Periodic KYC updation is risk-based (2, 8 or 10 years). For individuals with no change, a self-declaration suffices. Where documents are not as per current CDD standards, or have expired, fresh KYC is required. Aadhaar OTP e-KYC may be used, and the NBFC must update records and acknowledge the customer.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Do not rely on stored Aadhaar images for re-KYC. Use self-declaration, Aadhaar OTP e-KYC or other permitted modes, and do fresh KYC where documents are expired or non-compliant. Document the approach in the Board-approved KYC policy.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 1 of 5, pp. 40-41 (passage 1606)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 2 of 5, pp. 41-42 (passage 1607)

### 5. [LOW] Records of customer identification and address must be kept for at least five years after the business relationship has ended. Transaction records must be kept for at least five years from the date of the transaction.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Replace the indefinite retention with a defined schedule that runs five years from the end of the business relationship. Keep only the records required (for example, masked copies) and delete them after that period.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 47, pp. 48-49 (passage 1616)

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

We complete KYC once at onboarding and never update it afterwards, including for customers our risk engine classifies as high risk.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Does the RBI KYC Directions for NBFCs require periodic updation of KYC, and what is the prescribed frequency for each risk category (high, medium, low risk customers)?
- **q2** Is an NBFC required to apply ongoing due diligence and risk-based monitoring of customer accounts after onboarding, and must high-risk customers be subject to enhanced due diligence and more frequent review?
- **q3** What procedure and timelines must an NBFC follow for KYC updation, including customer-initiated updates, no-change self-declarations, and consequences of failing to update (such as restrictions on accounts)?
- **q4** Must an NBFC conduct periodic review of customer risk categorisation and obtain fresh or updated customer identification data when there are triggers such as doubts about the veracity of previously obtained data?
- **q5** Does the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025 require the NBFC as data fiduciary to keep personal data accurate and complete and to retain KYC data only as long as needed, which bears on never refreshing KYC records?

## Findings (4)

### 1. [HIGH] The NBFC must carry out periodic KYC updation at least once every two years for high-risk customers, every eight years for medium-risk and every ten years for low-risk customers, counted from account opening or last updation. The policy must be documented in the Board-approved KYC policy.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Build periodic KYC updation into the product with a two-year cycle for high-risk, eight-year for medium-risk and ten-year for low-risk customers. Document it in the Board-approved KYC policy. Identify and remediate existing customers whose updation is overdue.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 1 of 5, pp. 40-41 (passage 1606)

### 2. [HIGH] The NBFC must align monitoring with each customer's risk category and subject high-risk accounts to more intensified monitoring. It must also review risk categorisation at least every six months and decide whether enhanced due diligence is needed.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Put in place a periodic risk-categorisation review at least every six months. Trigger enhanced due diligence and intensified monitoring for high-risk customers, and make sure ongoing due diligence checks transactions against the customer's profile and source of funds.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 41, p. 40 (passage 1605)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 39, p. 40 (passage 1603)

### 3. [MEDIUM] For updation, the NBFC must obtain a self-declaration where nothing has changed, verify a changed address within two months, and ensure KYC documents meet current CDD standards. It must also acknowledge receipt of documents, promptly update its records, and intimate the customer of the date of updation.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Build updation workflows covering no-change self-declaration, change of address with verification within two months, acknowledgment and customer intimation, and re-KYC when documents are outdated or expired. Document these in the Board-approved policy.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 4 of 5, p. 43 (passage 1609)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 1 of 5, pp. 40-41 (passage 1606)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 2 of 5, pp. 41-42 (passage 1607)

### 4. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must review risk categorisation at least every six months. It must also carry out identification afresh when there is doubt about the authenticity or adequacy of previously obtained customer identification data.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Add event-based triggers for re-identification, such as doubts about the authenticity or adequacy of KYC data, alongside the scheduled six-monthly risk review. Feed the results back into the customer's risk category.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 21, p. 22 (passage 1574)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 41, p. 40 (passage 1605)

## Research limits reached

- q3: stopped after 4 research turns.

# Compliance review

## Feature

We are adding a dark mode toggle and a larger font option to the settings screen of our app. The choice is stored on the device only.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Does storing a user's display preferences (dark mode, font size) only on the user's own device, without transmitting it to the NBFC, amount to processing digital personal data of the Data Principal that requires notice and consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025?

## Findings (0)

No verified findings: the retrieved regulation states no obligation this feature touches.

6. Reasonable security safeguards. — (1) A Data Fiduciary shall protect personal data in its possession or
under its control, including in respect of any processing undertaken by it or on its behalf by a Data
Processor, by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach, which shall include, at
the minimum, —
(a) appropriate data security measures, such as securing of personal data through encryption,

such a Data Processor, wherever applicable;

for enabling detection of unauthorised access, its investigation and remediation to prevent

availability of such personal data being compromised as a result of destruction or loss of access to
personal data or otherwise, such as by way of data-backups;

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

An internal tool lets our head-office employees book desks and meeting rooms for the week. It shows room names and time slots only.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Does an internal desk and meeting room booking tool that records only employee room names and time slots fall outside the scope of the RBI NBFC KYC, Credit Facilities (digital lending) and Responsible Business Conduct Directions 2025, given that it involves no customers, loans or borrower data?
- **q2** If the booking tool links room reservations to identifiable employees (such as names or employee IDs), does this count as processing digital personal data under the DPDP Rules 2025, and what obligations does the NBFC have as data fiduciary (notice, purpose limitation, reasonable security safeguards, erasure after purpose is served)?

## Findings (4)

### 1. [MEDIUM] If bookings are linked to identifiable employees (names or IDs), the NBFC as Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards. At minimum these include encryption, masking or tokenisation, access controls, logs and monitoring, backups, and retention of logs and personal data for one year to detect and investigate unauthorised access.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: If employee identifiers are stored, apply access controls, logging and monitoring, and backups to the booking tool. Retain the logs for one year. If a vendor hosts the tool, include security safeguards in the contract.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 6, p. 26 (passage 1965)

### 2. [MEDIUM] The notice to the Data Principal must be clear and standalone. It must give an itemised description of the personal data and the specified purpose of processing. It must also give a link to the Data Fiduciary's website or app and describe how to withdraw consent, exercise rights and complain to the Board.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: If bookings carry employee names or IDs, give employees a short notice. It should list the data collected (name, ID, time slots), state the purpose (desk and room booking), and explain how to exercise rights or complain. Check whether another lawful basis applies to employee data.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 3, pp. 24-25 (passage 1962)

### 3. [LOW] The NBFC KYC Directions apply to all NBFCs, but not to NBFCs with no customer interface. They concern customer due diligence, so they have no bearing on an internal tool that records only room names and time slots.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Record that the room booking tool is an internal employee facility with no customer or borrower data and is outside KYC scope. Confirm that it stays separate from customer-facing systems and customer data. Note that the other RBI Directions apply in addition to other laws (Responsible Business Conduct Para 108), so this scoping does not exempt the tool from DPDP.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 3, p. 3 (passage 1542)

### 4. [LOW] Data Fiduciaries must publish business contact details of the person who can answer questions about processing, and include them in every response to a rights request.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Confirm that the NBFC's published contact details for data queries cover employee data in the booking tool.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 9, p. 27 (passage 1969)

LSP is need-based and with prior and explicit consent of the borrower having
audit trail. In any case, an NBFC shall also ensure that DLA of NBFC / LSP
desist from accessing mobile phone resources like file and media, contact list,
call logs, telephony functions, etc. A one-time access can be taken for camera,
microphone, location or any other facility necessary for the purpose of on-
boarding / KYC requirements only, with the explicit consent of the borrower.
(2) The borrower shall be provided with an option to give or deny consent for use
of specific data, restrict disclosure to third parties, data retention, revoke
consent already granted to collect personal data and if required, make the
NBFC / LSP delete / forget the data.

stage of interface with the borrowers.
